content.title: Noun Number, Possessives, and Determiner Agreement
content.overview: This guide covers core SAT concepts regarding noun forms, including distinguishing between singular and plural forms, the correct construction of possessives, and the logical matching between nouns and determiners (such as articles and demonstrative pronouns).
learning_objectives: Accurately distinguish between singular and plural noun forms
Master the use of apostrophes for singular and plural noun possessives
Identify and correct inconsistencies between nouns and their determiners (e.g., a, an, this, these)
Distinguish spelling differences between plural forms and possessive forms

sections.title: Basics of Noun Number
sections.content: The number of a noun must be consistent with the context. Singular nouns refer to one thing, while plural nouns refer to multiple things. On the SAT, students must determine whether a noun should be singular or plural based on quantifiers (such as 'many', 'each', 'one of the') or verb forms. For example, 'one of the' must be followed by a plural noun (one of the students).

sections.title: Rules for Forming Possessives
sections.content: Possessives are used to show ownership. The basic rules are: 1. Singular noun possessive: Add 's to the end of the word (e.g., the director's office). Even for singular nouns ending in s, 's is usually added. 2. Plural noun possessive: For plural nouns ending in s, add only an apostrophe ' (e.g., the students' grades); for irregular plural nouns not ending in s, add 's (e.g., the children's toys).

sections.title: Determiner Agreement and Consistency
sections.content: Determiners must agree with the number of the noun. Singular determiners (a, an, this, that, each, every) modify singular countable nouns; plural determiners (these, those, many, several, few) modify plural nouns. Uncountable nouns are usually treated as singular and use singular determiners (this information, much water).

sections.title: Distinguishing Confusing Forms
sections.content: Students often confuse plural forms (-s/-es) with possessive forms (-'s/-s'). Plural forms only indicate quantity and do not contain an apostrophe; possessive forms must contain an apostrophe to indicate ownership. For example: 'The scientists (plural) conducted research' vs 'The scientist's (singular possessive) discovery' vs 'The scientists' (plural possessive) lab'.

worked_examples.question: Choose the correct forms in the parentheses: The (A. artist's / B. artists) paintings were displayed in the gallery, showcasing the (C. woman's / D. womens') unique style.
worked_examples.solution: First part: Based on 'paintings' and 'were', this refers to the ownership of the paintings, typically by one or more artists. If referring to one artist, choose A (artist's). Second part: The plural of 'woman' is 'women', so its possessive should be 'women's'. Option D is spelled incorrectly, so choose C (woman's).

worked_examples.question: Correct the error: Each students must bring their own laptop to the seminar.
worked_examples.solution: The error is that the determiner 'Each' must be followed by a singular noun. It should be changed to 'Each student'. Note: Although 'their' is often used to refer to 'each student' in spoken English, in strict grammar exams, the noun's number must first match the determiner.

common_mistakes: Incorrectly adding an apostrophe to a standard plural noun (e.g., writing 'two books' as 'two book's').
Confusing 'its' (possessive pronoun, no apostrophe) with 'it's' (contraction of 'it is').
Using a singular noun after the 'one of the...' structure.
Misplacing the plural possessive apostrophe, such as writing the possessive of 'teachers' (plural) as 'teacher's' (singular possessive).
exam_tips: When you see an apostrophe, immediately ask yourself: Is this showing 'ownership'? If it just means 'multiple', no apostrophe is needed.
Check the determiner before the noun: this/that corresponds to singular, these/those corresponds to plural.
Watch for irregular plurals: The possessives of people, children, men, and women always add 's.
content.recap: The key to mastering noun number, possessives, and determiner agreement is to observe quantity clues in the context, strictly follow apostrophe rules, and ensure logical consistency in number between determiners and nouns.

knowledge_claims.content: The possessive of a singular noun is formed by adding an apostrophe and the letter s ('s) to the end of the word.
For plural nouns ending in s, the possessive is formed by adding only an apostrophe (') to the end of the word.
Irregular plural nouns that do not end in s (e.g., children, people) form their possessive by adding 's.
Simple plural forms (indicating multiple) do not use apostrophes, whereas possessive forms (indicating ownership) must use apostrophes.
The determiners 'each' and 'every' must be followed by a singular countable noun.
The demonstrative pronouns 'these' and 'those' must modify plural nouns.
The phrase 'one of the' must be followed by a plural noun to indicate one individual out of a group.
Misusing 'it's' (it is) as a possessive is a common error; 'its' is the correct possessive form and does not have an apostrophe.
A way to determine if a possessive should be used is to see if the noun is immediately followed by another noun or concept that it owns.
On the SAT, the number of a noun must be logically consistent with quantity clues provided in the sentence (e.g., many, single, various).
